questions.stem: Which of the following best defines organisational change?
options: A significant alteration to the structure, culture, processes or strategy of a business
Any day-to-day variation in the number of orders received
A change in the share price of a listed company
A change in the rate of corporation tax
questions.why: Organisational change refers to significant internal alteration, not to routine fluctuation or external conditions.
whyNot: Normal fluctuations in demand are not organisational change.
Share price movement is a market outcome, not a change in the organisation.
A tax change is an external influence that may cause change but is not itself organisational.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines delayering?
options: Removing one or more levels of management from the hierarchy
Reducing the total number of employees across the business
Moving from a functional to a divisional structure
Employing more staff on temporary contracts
questions.why: Delayering removes a level of management, which widens spans of control for those who remain.
whyNot: That is downsizing, which reduces headcount without necessarily removing a level.
That is restructuring, which changes the shape rather than the number of levels.
That is a move towards a flexible workforce.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a flexible workforce?
options: A workforce whose size, hours or skills can be varied to match changing needs
A workforce that is paid entirely by results
A workforce with no formal contracts of employment
A workforce that works only from home
questions.why: Flexibility comes from part-time, temporary, multi-skilled, flexible-hours and outsourced working.
whyNot: Payment method is a reward issue, not a measure of flexibility.
Flexible workers still have contracts, though the terms differ.
Homeworking is one form of flexibility, not the definition of it.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines resistance to change?
options: Opposition by employees or managers to a proposed change in the business
The time taken for a change to be fully implemented
The cost of training employees in new methods
The legal restrictions on changing employment contracts
questions.why: Resistance is opposition from inside the organisation, and it has identifiable causes.
whyNot: That is the implementation period, not opposition to the change.
Training cost is a cost of change rather than resistance to it.
Legal constraints are external, not internal opposition.

questions.stem: Why is imposed change harder to manage than planned change?
options: There is no time to prepare people, resource the change or communicate the reasons
Imposed change is always larger in scale
Imposed change is always illegal
Imposed change never affects employees
questions.why: Planned change is chosen, timed and resourced; imposed change arrives whether the business is ready or not, which is the whole argument for being flexible in advance.
whyNot: Scale varies; the difficulty comes from the absence of preparation time.
Change forced by events such as a recession is not unlawful.
Imposed change usually affects employees most of all.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a disadvantage of delayering?
options: Wider spans of control stretch the remaining managers and career paths disappear
It increases the number of levels in the hierarchy
It always raises total costs
It slows communication between the top and the bottom
questions.why: Removing a level increases the load on those who remain, and it takes away promotion steps, which weakens the succession pipeline.
whyNot: Delayering reduces the number of levels by definition.
It usually reduces costs, which is the main reason it is done.
It typically speeds communication by shortening the chain.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a disadvantage of a flexible workforce?
options: Insecurity damages motivation and loyalty, and temporary staff are less trained
It raises the business's fixed costs
It makes the business slower to respond to demand changes
It prevents multi-skilling
questions.why: Flexibility is bought at the cost of commitment, and the ethical objections about insecure work also apply.
whyNot: It lowers fixed costs by converting them towards variable costs.
It makes the business faster to respond, which is its main benefit.
Multi-skilling is one of the ways flexibility is achieved.

questions.stem: Which group typically resists delayering most strongly, and why?
options: Middle managers, because their authority came from the level being removed
New recruits, because they have the least experience
Shareholders, because costs will fall
Customers, because prices may fall
questions.why: Those whose status and authority depend on the existing hierarchy have the most to lose.
whyNot: New recruits have least invested in the old structure.
Shareholders generally welcome lower costs.
Customers are not usually affected by internal layers.

questions.stem: Why should a business explain why a change is happening, not just what will change?
options: People accept change more readily when they understand the reason for it
Explaining the reason removes the need for any training
The law requires an explanation of all business decisions
It guarantees that nobody will oppose the change
questions.why: Managing information is central to managing change, and the reason is the part that converts compliance into acceptance.
whyNot: Training is still needed wherever new skills are required.
There is no such general legal requirement.
Some opposition is likely regardless; good communication reduces it rather than removing it.

questions.stem: What happens when a business delays communicating a change?
options: Staff fill the gap with rumours that are usually worse than the truth
Staff lose interest in the change entirely
Resistance disappears because there is nothing to react to
The change becomes cheaper to implement
questions.why: In the absence of information people invent their own version, so early communication is a practical necessity rather than a courtesy.
whyNot: Uncertainty about job security raises anxiety rather than indifference.
Uncertainty increases resistance rather than removing it.
Poorly communicated change usually costs more through lost productivity.

questions.stem: In Lewin's force field analysis, which action is usually more effective?
options: Weakening the restraining forces, for example by removing a specific fear through training
Strengthening the driving forces by increasing pressure on staff
Removing the driving forces so the change becomes voluntary
Increasing both sets of forces equally
questions.why: Removing a restrainer removes the resistance itself, whereas adding pressure to a resisting organisation raises tension on both sides.
whyNot: More pressure tends to provoke more resistance rather than overcoming it.
Removing the drivers would stop the change from happening at all.
Raising both leaves the balance unchanged and the organisation under strain.

questions.stem: A force field analysis scores driving forces at 14 and restraining forces at 19. What does this suggest?
options: The change is likely to stall unless the restraining forces are reduced
The change will proceed smoothly as planned
The scores prove the change should be abandoned permanently
The analysis cannot be used to draw any conclusion
questions.why: Restrainers outweigh drivers, so the change will not move until the balance is altered, most cheaply by addressing the restrainers.
whyNot: A change facing stronger restraint than drive does not proceed smoothly.
It shows the change cannot proceed as currently planned, not that it is wrong in principle.
Comparing the totals is precisely the conclusion the technique is designed to give.

questions.stem: Why can dismissing employee objections as mere resistance be a serious management error?
options: The people doing the work may be able to see that the plan will not work
Employees have a legal right to veto changes
Resistance always disappears if it is ignored
Objections are never related to the change itself
questions.why: Resistance sometimes contains genuine information the plan needs, which is why consultation is a source of intelligence and not just a way to build acceptance.
whyNot: Employees generally have consultation rights rather than a veto.
Ignored resistance tends to persist and to reappear during implementation.
Objections are usually specific to the change being proposed.

questions.stem: What is the most common weakness in relying on communication alone to deliver change?
options: Staff judge the change by behaviour and rewards, not by announcements
Communication is prohibitively expensive
Communication increases resistance in every case
Communication is only possible in small businesses
questions.why: Communication is necessary and not sufficient: if rewards and management behaviour do not change, staff conclude that nothing has.
whyNot: Communication is one of the cheapest elements of a change programme.
Good communication generally reduces resistance.
Large businesses communicate change routinely, though it is harder.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of force field analysis?
options: The scores are subjective and it gives a snapshot rather than showing how forces interact
It requires audited financial statements
It can only be used for changes costing under $1m
It cannot be applied to organisational change
questions.why: It is a useful structuring tool whose weightings depend on judgement, and it does not show how the forces affect one another over time.
whyNot: It uses management judgement, not financial statements.
There is no cost limit on its use.
Organisational change is exactly what it was designed for.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a benefit of restructuring?
options: It can fit the structure to the strategy and bring decisions closer to customers
It removes the need to communicate with employees
It reduces the number of employees automatically
It guarantees a fall in total costs
questions.why: Restructuring aligns the shape of the organisation with what the strategy requires, for example moving to divisions as the business expands internationally.
whyNot: Restructuring makes communication more important, not less.
It changes the shape rather than necessarily the headcount.
It can duplicate functions and raise costs in the short term.
